kp.k: Statistical evaluation targets generalization beyond fixed benchmarks
kp.d: This June 1, 2026 arXiv preprint develops a theoretical framework for generative-model evaluation, rather than providing empirical findings about legal services. The authors distinguish held-out IID statistical evaluation from fixed-task benchmarks and costly human feedback. They present statistical evaluation as a scalable complement to those approaches, while acknowledging its inability to capture some qualitative aspects of model behavior.
qs: By statistical evaluation, we mean assessing models using held-out IID data drawn from a ground truth distribution.
While benchmarks provide standardized and interpretable comparisons, they assess performance on a fixed set of tasks, making it difficult to reason about generalization beyond the benchmark.
Human feedback, in contrast, requires costly human labor.

kp.k: Ranking models differs from estimating metric values
kp.d: The framework asks whether an algorithm supplied with two candidate models and finite IID ground-truth samples can reliably select a model whose population metric is sufficiently close to the better candidate's. Strong evaluability permits arbitrary additive error; c-weak evaluability additionally permits a multiplicative factor c. These are uniform guarantees across candidate pairs and ground truths, not claims that a particular evaluation dataset establishes model quality. Estimability implies strong evaluability, but the authors leave the converse open.
qs: We introduce two levels of evaluability: a metric is strongly evaluable if it can be evaluated with arbitrary precision from finite samples, and weakly evaluable if it can be evaluated up to multiplicative and additive approximation errors.
It is unclear whether the converse holds true.

kp.k: Binary test complexity determines attainable ranking accuracy
kp.d: Theorem 3.2 states that integral probability metrics over binary tests are estimable and strongly evaluable when the test class has finite VC dimension. With unbounded VC dimension, they remain 3-weakly evaluable, but no multiplicative factor below 3 is possible. Thus approximate candidate selection can remain feasible even where precise metric estimation is impossible. Total variation is the special case containing all binary tests.
qs: Note that when F contains all binary functions, the corresponding IPM is the TV distance.
In contrast, when the test class has unbounded VC dimension, strong evaluability is impossible, yet a weaker form of evaluability remains achievable.
In other words, we can still have a coarse ranking of models even when estimating the IPM is not possible.

kp.k: Bounded real-valued tests support conditional precision
kp.d: For test functions valued in [0, 1], Proposition 3.4 establishes estimability and strong evaluability when the fat-shattering dimension is finite at every positive scale. Bounded IPMs retain factor-3 weak evaluability even without that complexity restriction. Unlike the binary case, the authors do not establish that factor 3 is optimal for real-valued test classes with unbounded complexity.
qs: Bounded IPMs are always weakly evaluable, regardless of the complexity of the test class, providing a guarantee that these metrics can at least be evaluated approximately;
For bounded real-valued test classes, IPMs are strongly evaluable when the test class has finite γ-fat shattering dimension for all γ > 0 but it might require arbitrarily large sample size.
However, we were not able to prove that the factor of 3 is optimal, which would mirror our result in the case where the test class is binary-valued.

kp.k: Evaluability need not imply manageable sample requirements
kp.d: Theorem 3.6 claims that estimable IPMs do not admit a finite taxonomy of sample complexities; the paper's definition encompasses finite or countable lists of candidate rate functions. The authors contrast this with supervised learning's familiar VC-dimension-based rates, emphasizing that finite-sample estimability can coexist with arbitrarily demanding accuracy-dependent sample requirements.
qs: There does not exist a finite taxonomy of sample complexities for estimable IPMs.

One might hope that estimable metrics admit a finite number of sample-complexity behaviors, so that every estimable metric can be evaluated with sample complexity comparable to one of a fixed collection of functions of the desired accuracy.

kp.k: Unbounded single tests can defeat reliable evaluation
kp.d: Theorem 3.8 examines the absolute difference between a fixed test's expectations under model and ground truth. If the test is uniformly bounded by B, the metric is estimable and strongly evaluable with sample complexity O(B² log(1/δ)/ε²). Under the stated unboundedness condition—a finite nonzero test value and other values arbitrarily larger in magnitude—the metric is not weakly evaluable. The lower-bound construction uses low-probability observations with disproportionately large test values.
qs: In Section 3.2, we consider a single fixed but possibly unbounded test and discuss the dependency of evaluability on the magnitude of the test function.

kp.k: Rare-event sensitivity prevents uniform divergence evaluation
kp.d: Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.3 establish that Rényi divergences with α > 1 and KL divergence are not weakly evaluable under the unrestricted framework. The constructions make candidate distributions nearly indistinguishable in finite samples while producing large divergence differences through tiny assigned probabilities. These are worst-case theoretical impossibility results, not measured failure rates for deployed models. Extension to broader tail-sensitive f-divergences is explicitly conjectural, and total variation is a counterexample to extending the result to all f-divergences.
qs: These two divergences share a common pathology that our construction exploits — their value can become unbounded if a model places negligible mass compared to the ground truth on even a single point.
In this sense, these divergences penalize undercoverage of the ground-truth distribution rather than generic mismatch.
We believe that our negative results for the α-Rényi and KL divergences extend to a broader subclass of tail-sensitive f -divergences.

kp.k: Truncation introduces threshold problems unless margins are imposed
kp.d: The coverage profile measures ground-truth probability mass where the ground-truth-to-model likelihood ratio reaches a threshold N. Proposition 4.5 establishes non-weak-evaluability for N ≥ 2, even with a positive lower bound on ground-truth support probabilities: threshold discontinuity can make nearly indistinguishable ground truths reverse candidate rankings. Theorem 4.8 recovers strong-evaluability-style guarantees only when ground-truth support probabilities have a fixed positive lower bound and both candidates' likelihood ratios remain a fixed positive distance from N.
qs: Hence, models that are indistinguishable with finite samples could actually have very different coverage profiles.
The difference is that rather than the result holding for all possible ground truths and pairs of candidate models, it only holds in settings where Assumption 4.6 and Assumption 4.7 are satisfied.

kp.k: Perplexity can misrank distributionally better models
kp.d: The authors analyze negative log-likelihood because exponentiation to perplexity preserves candidate rankings. Theorem 5.3 shows that this score cannot weakly evaluate total variation or β-restricted KL divergence for β in (0, 1/2). The mechanism is metric-score mismatch: negative log-likelihood amplifies extremely small model probabilities, whereas total variation is bounded and restricted KL can disregard up to β ground-truth mass. This limitation of perplexity does not negate total variation's factor-3 evaluability using other algorithms.
qs: since perplexity is simply the exponential of the nll, both scores induce the same ordering over models and are therefore equivalent for the purposes of evaluability.
A single data point that is assigned extremely small probability by q dominates the score, regardless of the model’s behavior on the rest of the distribution.
Metrics that tolerate rare errors cannot be evaluated by scores that amplify them.

kp.k: Perplexity gains guarantees under restrictive candidate assumptions
kp.d: Proposition 5.6 recovers additive-ε total-variation ranking guarantees for negative log-likelihood when at least one candidate is pointwise within factors 1 − Δ and 1 + Δ of the ground-truth probabilities, with Δ ≤ O(ε²). The stated sample requirement is O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)). This is a conditional, semi-realizable result, not a general endorsement of perplexity or an empirical finding that practical models satisfy the assumption.
qs: Fundamentally, Assumption 5.5 transforms our setting into a semi-realizable one and ensures that one of the models must achieve a bounded nll score close to that of q ⋆ .
However, our results highlight that perplexity cannot be used blindly as an evaluation method without a principled understanding of the underlying candidate models that it is used to rank.

kp.k: Restricted KL leaves weak evaluability unresolved
kp.d: The β-restricted KL metric minimizes a restricted positive average log-likelihood ratio over subsets carrying at least 1 − β ground-truth mass; it is not simply KL between conditional distributions. Theorem 5.4 rules out strong evaluability by any algorithm, while general weak evaluability beyond negative log-likelihood remains open. The authors identify discontinuous changes in admissible subsets as an additional obstacle and report no non-degenerate assumption restoring negative-log-likelihood evaluation beyond assuming a candidate equals ground truth.
qs: This is an unnormalized restriction of the KL integrand rather than explicitly being a KL divergence between the conditional distributions.
The metric allows us to ignore arbitrary subsets of mass, and as β changes, these subsets can look very different.
Any general evaluability guarantees for the β-restricted KL beyond the nll score are left as an open question.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Aiyer, Mansour, Moran and Shao claim that reliable finite-sample comparison of generative models depends on the evaluation metric; their claims concern machine-learning evaluation, not legal services.
pts.d: The authors distinguish evaluability—selecting between two candidate models with a high-probability approximation guarantee—from estimability, which approximates a metric's numerical value. Strong evaluability permits arbitrary additive accuracy; weak evaluability additionally permits multiplicative error. They argue that statistical evaluation complements benchmarks and human feedback by targeting generalization to an underlying distribution. These are methodological claims rather than forecasts of professional or market transformation.

pts.k: Bounded test-based metrics allow approximate model comparison, while sufficiently limited test-class complexity permits arbitrarily accurate comparison.
pts.d: The authors report that IPMs over bounded tests are always 3-weakly evaluable. For binary tests, finite VC dimension permits estimation and strong evaluation; unbounded VC dimension permits factor-3 weak evaluation but no better multiplicative guarantee. For bounded real-valued tests, finite fat-shattering dimension at every positive scale is sufficient for strong evaluation; optimality of factor 3 in the unbounded-complexity case remains open. They also claim that estimable IPMs can require arbitrarily large sample sizes and admit no finite or countable taxonomy of sample-complexity rates under their definition. For a single fixed test, boundedness permits strong evaluation, whereas the specified unboundedness condition prevents even weak evaluation.

pts.k: Rényi divergences of order greater than one and KL divergence cannot support uniformly reliable finite-sample model ranking in the unrestricted framework; truncation does not automatically solve the problem.
pts.d: The authors attribute the Rényi and KL impossibility results to rare points on which a candidate assigns vanishingly small probability relative to ground truth. For the coverage profile at thresholds N ≥ 2, they identify threshold discontinuity as an additional obstacle: arbitrarily similar ground truths can reverse the preferred candidate. They explicitly do not extend the impossibility claim to all distributional distances, since total variation permits factor-3 weak evaluation. Their suggested extension to a broader class of tail-sensitive f-divergences is a conjecture, not an established result.

pts.k: Perplexity can misrank models because its sensitivity to low-probability events is misaligned with the intended evaluation metric.
pts.d: The authors analyze negative log-likelihood (NLL), which induces the same ordering as perplexity. They claim that perplexity cannot generally evaluate cross-entropy/KL reliably and cannot weakly evaluate either total variation or their β-restricted KL metric. Separately, they report that β-restricted KL is not strongly evaluable by any algorithm in the unrestricted setting; whether other algorithms can weakly evaluate it remains open. They recover an NLL-based total-variation comparison guarantee under a stringent closeness-to-ground-truth assumption and caution against treating perplexity as an unconditional measure of overall distributional similarity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is mathematical analysis and constructed counterexamples, supplemented by prior theoretical and empirical literature—not experiments on deployed legal or general-purpose AI products.
pts.d: The June 2026 arXiv preprint supplies definitions, theorems, propositions, proof sketches and appendix proofs. Positive results use uniform convergence, VC and fat-shattering dimensions, concentration bounds and earlier density-estimation algorithms. Negative results construct candidate distributions and ground truths whose finite-sample observations are difficult to distinguish despite materially different metric rankings. The coverage-profile argument uses nearby ground truths on opposite sides of a threshold; the perplexity arguments construct explicit ranking reversals. The authors cite Fang et al. (2025) and Hu et al. (2024) for empirical concerns about perplexity and downstream performance, but report no new empirical benchmark scores, measured error rates, legal cases or adoption data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims are theoretical results presented in the 1 June 2026 version, with no adoption or disruption horizon; their scope depends on IID sampling and explicit uniform guarantees.
pts.d: Evaluation receives two candidate probability distributions and held-out IID samples from a ground-truth distribution. The unrestricted definition requires a sample-size guarantee that works across every candidate pair and ground truth for specified accuracy, confidence and approximation factor. Consequently, non-evaluability denotes the absence of this uniform guarantee, not a claim that every fixed practical instance fails. Strong evaluation of binary IPMs requires finite VC dimension; the real-valued sufficient condition is finite fat-shattering dimension at every positive scale. Conditional coverage-profile evaluation requires both a positive lower bound on every ground-truth support probability and a fixed margin separating each candidate's likelihood ratios from threshold N. Conditional NLL evaluation of total variation requires at least one candidate to satisfy the pointwise ratio bounds (1−Δ)q⋆ ≤ q ≤ (1+Δ)q⋆, with Δ of order ε² or smaller; the stated sample size is O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)). These results establish statistical possibility, not a demonstrated practical implementation or runtime guarantee.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The implied affected groups are generative-model researchers, developers and evaluators choosing metrics and comparing models, particularly for pre-training and synthetic-data applications.
pts.d: The source identifies evaluation settings rather than occupational or market segments. Its implications concern which population-level comparisons evaluators can justify from test samples, the amount of data required, and the risk of choosing an unsuitable score or metric. It presents statistical evaluation as inexpensive and scalable relative to human feedback, while acknowledging its qualitative limitations. It makes no claims about law-firm staffing, legal-service prices, legal-AI vendors, clients' access to justice or human verification of legal outputs; those would be extrapolations beyond this cross-domain source.
